Rigorous Derivation of the Jitter Kernels: TIE, N-period, cycle-to-cycle

Prerequisites: psd_phase_noise_jitter · stochastic_noise_basics · dsp_view_of_phase_noise ｜ Next: allan_variance · serdes_clocking_connection

psd_phase_noise_jitter already gave the "operational versions" of the three jitter weighting kernels; this page derives them rigorously from first principles, and answers the question that has been left hanging: what exactly is the prefactor? Which 2 belongs to which convention? The answer is calibrated with three independent rulers: (1) the step-by-step derivation, (2) exact agreement with the verified σΔϕ=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta\phi}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔϕ​=κΔt​ of [P2], (3) Monte-Carlo time-domain measurement (simulations/lab_24_jitter_kernels.py) — all three agree to ~0.1%.

This page supersedes the earlier external-convention TODO: this site previously marked the prefactor of the period-jitter kernel in worked_examples Example C3 as "external literature, to be confirmed". This page has now derived it from first principles and verified it by Monte Carlo: under the "one-sided SϕS_\phiSϕ​, ∫0∞\int_0^\infty∫0∞​" convention the prefactor is exactly 1/ω021/\omega_0^21/ω02​ (not 2/ω022/\omega_0^22/ω02​ — that 2 belongs to the two-sided-spectrum or L=12Sϕ\mathcal{L}=\tfrac12 S_\phiL=21​Sϕ​ bookkeeping; see the conversion table in Step 0). The kernel and constant used in Example C3 are correct; its value 27.6 fs is the closed-form 28.28 fs after truncating the band to 10310^3103–101010^{10}1010 Hz (Section 7 of this page has markers reconciling each number).

Physical intuition (conclusion first): the three jitters are three ways of reading the same phase process ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) — read it directly (TIE), read the difference NNN beats apart (N-period), or read the difference of adjacent differences (cycle-to-cycle). In the frequency domain, "taking a difference" is multiplication by a deterministic filter; multiply Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) by that filter's ∣H∣2\lvert H\rvert^2∣H∣2 and integrate, and you get that jitter's variance. The kernel's shape decides "which part of the frequency axis of the phase noise gets counted": TIE eats the low end, period is a first-order high-pass, c2c is a second-order high-pass. Every 2 and 4 can be traced to its origin.

Step 0: declaration of the single convention (the foundation of every formula on this page)​

This page uses exactly one convention: Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) is the one-sided power spectral density of the excess phase, in rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz, defined for f≥0f\ge0f≥0; all integrals are ∫0∞df\int_0^\infty df∫0∞​df. Its relation to the variance is

σϕ2=∫0∞Sϕ(f) df[rad2].\sigma_\phi^2=\int_0^\infty S_\phi(f)\,df\qquad[\text{rad}^2].σϕ2​=∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)df[rad2].

No extra factor of 2 anywhere. Other conventions common in the literature convert as follows (same physical quantity, three bookkeepings; SϕDS=Sϕ/2S_\phi^{DS}=S_\phi/2SϕDS​=Sϕ​/2 is the two-sided spectrum, Llin=12Sϕ\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}=\tfrac12 S_\phiLlin​=21​Sϕ​ is the small-angle SSB; see the derivation in psd_phase_noise_jitter):

  • In the versions written in the literature as 2ω02∫Sϕ⋅4sin⁡2df\frac{2}{\omega_0^2}\int S_\phi\cdot4\sin^2 dfω02​2​∫Sϕ​⋅4sin2df, the SϕS_\phiSϕ​ is either a two-sided spectrum or is L\mathcal{L}L relabeled as SϕS_\phiSϕ​; plugging a one-sided spectrum into that formula overcounts the variance by 2× (jitter by 2\sqrt22​). That was exactly the sticking point behind Example C3's original TODO, and one more case of this site's factor-of-2 discipline (cf. the SSB /4/4/4 vs time-domain /2/2/2 note in Section 3 of the conventions).

Step 1: edge timing error = a sample of the phase (time-domain starting point)​

The total phase of the oscillator output is Φ(t)=ω0t+ϕ(t)\Phi(t)=\omega_0 t+\phi(t)Φ(t)=ω0​t+ϕ(t) (the phase term of [P1] Eq.(1), p.181; ϕ\phiϕ is the excess phase, rad). The kkk-th rising zero crossing tkt_ktk​ is defined by "the total phase has completed kkk full turns":

ω0tk+ϕ(tk)=2πk.\omega_0 t_k+\phi(t_k)=2\pi k.ω0​tk​+ϕ(tk​)=2πk.

Solve for tkt_ktk​ (treat ϕ\phiϕ as a small perturbation and expand to first order about tk=kTt_k=kTtk​=kT):

tk=kT−ϕ(tk)ω0≈kT−ϕ(kT)ω0.t_k=kT-\frac{\phi(t_k)}{\omega_0}\approx kT-\frac{\phi(kT)}{\omega_0}.tk​=kT−ω0​ϕ(tk​)​≈kT−ω0​ϕ(kT)​.
  • Approximation used: first-order expansion; requires the effect of ∣ϕ(tk)−ϕ(kT)∣≪∣ϕ(kT)∣\lvert\phi(t_k)-\phi(kT)\rvert\ll\lvert\phi(kT)\rvert∣ϕ(tk​)−ϕ(kT)∣≪∣ϕ(kT)∣ to be negligible, equivalent to ∣ϕ˙∣≪ω0\lvert\dot\phi\rvert\ll\omega_0∣ϕ˙​∣≪ω0​ (instantaneous frequency offset far below the carrier) and σt≪T\sigma_t\ll Tσt​≪T (jitter far smaller than the period). Practical oscillators have fs-level jitter with periods of hundreds of ps, so this holds easily.
  • Failure conditions: cycle slips (Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ accumulating to ∼\sim∼rad within one correlation time), strong injection pulling, or non-negligible AM-PM conversion — then edges and phase are no longer one-to-one.
  • Units: [ϕ/ω0]=rad/(rad/s)=s[\phi/\omega_0]=\text{rad}/(\text{rad/s})=\text{s}[ϕ/ω0​]=rad/(rad/s)=s ✓.

So the timing error of the kkk-th edge (TIE, time interval error, deviation from the ideal clock) is

TIEk=tk−kT=−ϕ(kT)ω0.\text{TIE}_k=t_k-kT=-\frac{\phi(kT)}{\omega_0}.TIEk​=tk​−kT=−ω0​ϕ(kT)​.

The minus sign just says "phase leads = edge arrives early"; after taking the variance it affects nothing.

Step 2: three jitters = 0th/1st/2nd-order differences of the phase​

Following the definitions of notation (conventions Section 2), rewritten entirely in the language of ϕ\phiϕ:

TIE (absolute):TIEk=−ϕ(kT)ω0(0th order: direct sampling)N-period jitter:Pk(N)=(tk+N−tk)−NT=−ϕ((k+N)T)−ϕ(kT)ω0(1st-order difference, spacing NT)cycle-to-cycle:Ck=Tk+1−Tk=−ϕ((k+2)T)−2ϕ((k+1)T)+ϕ(kT)ω0(2nd-order difference).\begin{aligned} \text{TIE (absolute):}\quad &\text{TIE}_k=-\frac{\phi(kT)}{\omega_0} &&(\text{0th order: direct sampling})\\ \text{N-period jitter:}\quad &P_k(N)=\big(t_{k+N}-t_k\big)-NT=-\frac{\phi\big((k{+}N)T\big)-\phi(kT)}{\omega_0} &&(\text{1st-order difference, spacing }NT)\\ \text{cycle-to-cycle:}\quad &C_k=T_{k+1}-T_k=-\frac{\phi\big((k{+}2)T\big)-2\phi\big((k{+}1)T\big)+\phi(kT)}{\omega_0} &&(\text{2nd-order difference}). \end{aligned}TIE (absolute):N-period jitter:cycle-to-cycle:​TIEk​=−ω0​ϕ(kT)​Pk​(N)=(tk+N​−tk​)−NT=−ω0​ϕ((k+N)T)−ϕ(kT)​Ck​=Tk+1​−Tk​=−ω0​ϕ((k+2)T)−2ϕ((k+1)T)+ϕ(kT)​​​(0th order: direct sampling)(1st-order difference, spacing NT)(2nd-order difference).​

Pk(1)=Tk−TP_k(1)=T_k-TPk​(1)=Tk​−T at N=1N=1N=1 is what is commonly called the period jitter; CkC_kCk​ is the difference between two adjacent period lengths (the difference of the difference). All three are linear operations on ϕ\phiϕ, so the next step can process them all at once in the frequency domain.

Step 3: variance of a difference ← frequency-domain kernel (the core lemma, derived two ways)​

What we need is Var⁡[ϕ(t+τ0)−ϕ(t)]\operatorname{Var}\big[\phi(t+\tau_0)-\phi(t)\big]Var[ϕ(t+τ0​)−ϕ(t)] (τ0=NT\tau_0=NTτ0​=NT). Two mutually independent derivation routes follow; the second is mathematically stronger — it holds even when ϕ\phiϕ itself is a random walk (non-stationary).

Route A: assume ϕ\phiϕ wide-sense stationary (WSS), via the autocorrelation​

Step 1: expand the square. Let ϕ\phiϕ be WSS and zero-mean, with autocorrelation Rϕ(τ)=⟨ϕ(t)ϕ(t+τ)⟩R_\phi(\tau)=\langle\phi(t)\phi(t+\tau)\rangleRϕ​(τ)=⟨ϕ(t)ϕ(t+τ)⟩:

Var⁡[ϕ(t+τ0)−ϕ(t)]=⟨ϕ2(t+τ0)⟩+⟨ϕ2(t)⟩−2⟨ϕ(t)ϕ(t+τ0)⟩=2[Rϕ(0)−Rϕ(τ0)].\operatorname{Var}\big[\phi(t+\tau_0)-\phi(t)\big] =\big\langle\phi^2(t+\tau_0)\big\rangle+\big\langle\phi^2(t)\big\rangle-2\big\langle\phi(t)\phi(t+\tau_0)\big\rangle =2\big[R_\phi(0)-R_\phi(\tau_0)\big].Var[ϕ(t+τ0​)−ϕ(t)]=⟨ϕ2(t+τ0​)⟩+⟨ϕ2(t)⟩−2⟨ϕ(t)ϕ(t+τ0​)⟩=2[Rϕ​(0)−Rϕ​(τ0​)].

Step 2: Wiener–Khinchin. The autocorrelation representation with the one-sided spectrum (as in stochastic_noise_basics; [P2] takes this same Khinchin route on p.803, its Eq.(46)–(48)):

Rϕ(τ)=∫0∞Sϕ(f)cos⁡(2πfτ) df.R_\phi(\tau)=\int_0^\infty S_\phi(f)\cos(2\pi f\tau)\,df.Rϕ​(τ)=∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)cos(2πfτ)df.

Step 3: substitute back and use the half-angle identity. 1−cos⁡θ=2sin⁡2(θ/2)1-\cos\theta=2\sin^2(\theta/2)1−cosθ=2sin2(θ/2) with θ=2πfτ0\theta=2\pi f\tau_0θ=2πfτ0​:

Var⁡[Δϕ(τ0)]=2∫0∞Sϕ(f)[1−cos⁡(2πfτ0)]df=∫0∞Sϕ(f) 4sin⁡2(πfτ0)⏟kernel df.\operatorname{Var}\big[\Delta\phi(\tau_0)\big] =2\int_0^\infty S_\phi(f)\big[1-\cos(2\pi f\tau_0)\big]df =\int_0^\infty S_\phi(f)\,\underbrace{4\sin^2(\pi f\tau_0)}_{\text{kernel}}\,df.Var[Δϕ(τ0​)]=2∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)[1−cos(2πfτ0​)]df=∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)kernel4sin2(πfτ0​)​​df.

That is the entire origin of the 4sin⁡24\sin^24sin2 kernel: one factor of 2 comes from "variance of a difference =2[R(0)−R(τ0)]=2[R(0)-R(\tau_0)]=2[R(0)−R(τ0​)]", the other 2 from the half-angle identity; the two 2's multiply to 4, with not a single factor to spare. Equivalently, in filter language: y(t)=ϕ(t+τ0)−ϕ(t)y(t)=\phi(t+\tau_0)-\phi(t)y(t)=ϕ(t+τ0​)−ϕ(t) is LTI filtering with H(f)=ej2πfτ0−1H(f)=e^{j2\pi f\tau_0}-1H(f)=ej2πfτ0​−1,

∣H(f)∣2=(cos⁡(2πfτ0)−1)2+sin⁡2(2πfτ0)=2−2cos⁡(2πfτ0)=4sin⁡2(πfτ0),\lvert H(f)\rvert^2=\big(\cos(2\pi f\tau_0)-1\big)^2+\sin^2(2\pi f\tau_0)=2-2\cos(2\pi f\tau_0)=4\sin^2(\pi f\tau_0),∣H(f)∣2=(cos(2πfτ0​)−1)2+sin2(2πfτ0​)=2−2cos(2πfτ0​)=4sin2(πfτ0​),

and a WSS process through an LTI filter obeys Sy=∣H∣2SϕS_y=\lvert H\rvert^2S_\phiSy​=∣H∣2Sϕ​ (one-sided in, one-sided out); integrating gives the same formula.

Route B: no stationarity assumed for ϕ\phiϕ — only the "frequency noise" need be stationary (the rigorous version)​

Under white FM, ϕ\phiϕ is a random walk and Rϕ(0)R_\phi(0)Rϕ​(0) outright diverges, so strictly speaking Route A does not hold. But the increments are fine. Define the instantaneous frequency offset ν(t)≡ϕ˙(t)\nu(t)\equiv\dot\phi(t)ν(t)≡ϕ˙​(t) (rad/s), assume ν\nuν is WSS; its one-sided spectrum follows from the differentiation relation:

Sν(f)=(2πf)2 Sϕ(f)[(rad/s)2/Hz].S_\nu(f)=(2\pi f)^2\,S_\phi(f)\qquad[(\text{rad/s})^2/\text{Hz}].Sν​(f)=(2πf)2Sϕ​(f)[(rad/s)2/Hz].

Step 1: write the difference as a windowed integral of ν\nuν.

Δϕ(τ0)=ϕ(t+τ0)−ϕ(t)=∫tt+τ0ν(u) du,\Delta\phi(\tau_0)=\phi(t+\tau_0)-\phi(t)=\int_t^{t+\tau_0}\nu(u)\,du,Δϕ(τ0​)=ϕ(t+τ0​)−ϕ(t)=∫tt+τ0​​ν(u)du,

i.e., ν\nuν passes through a boxcar (rectangular-window) filter www of length τ0\tau_0τ0​.

Step 2: frequency response of the window.

W(f)=∫0τ0e−j2πfu du=1−e−j2πfτ0j2πf,∣W(f)∣2=4sin⁡2(πfτ0)(2πf)2[s2].W(f)=\int_0^{\tau_0}e^{-j2\pi fu}\,du=\frac{1-e^{-j2\pi f\tau_0}}{j2\pi f},\qquad \lvert W(f)\rvert^2=\frac{4\sin^2(\pi f\tau_0)}{(2\pi f)^2}\quad[\text{s}^2].W(f)=∫0τ0​​e−j2πfudu=j2πf1−e−j2πfτ0​​,∣W(f)∣2=(2πf)24sin2(πfτ0​)​[s2].

Step 3: combine. Var⁡[Δϕ]=∫0∞Sν∣W∣2df\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi]=\int_0^\infty S_\nu\lvert W\rvert^2dfVar[Δϕ]=∫0∞​Sν​∣W∣2df, and the (2πf)2(2\pi f)^2(2πf)2 cancels exactly:

Var⁡[Δϕ(τ0)]=∫0∞(2πf)2Sϕ(f)⋅4sin⁡2(πfτ0)(2πf)2 df=∫0∞Sϕ(f) 4sin⁡2(πfτ0) df.✓\operatorname{Var}\big[\Delta\phi(\tau_0)\big] =\int_0^\infty (2\pi f)^2 S_\phi(f)\cdot\frac{4\sin^2(\pi f\tau_0)}{(2\pi f)^2}\,df =\int_0^\infty S_\phi(f)\,4\sin^2(\pi f\tau_0)\,df.\qquad\checkmarkVar[Δϕ(τ0​)]=∫0␀∞​(2πf)2Sϕ​(f)⋅(2πf)24sin2(πfτ0​)​df=∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)4sin2(πfτ0​)df.✓

The same kernel, but this time only "ν\nuν stationary" was used — rigorously valid for 1/f21/f^21/f2 (white FM) and for 1/f31/f^31/f3 (flicker FM) once a cutoff is imposed. The kernel's f2f^2f2 zero at f→0f\to0f→0 is exactly the mechanism that makes the 1/f21/f^21/f2 spectrum integrable (the same trick as the difference kernel of allan_variance; the ADEV kernel 2sin⁡4(πfτ)/(πfτ)22\sin^4(\pi f\tau)/(\pi f\tau)^22sin4(πfτ)/(πfτ)2 is a relative — "gated average + adjacent difference").

  • dimension check (Route B): Sν [rad2s−2/Hz]×∣W∣2 [s2]×df [Hz]=rad2S_\nu\,[\text{rad}^2\text{s}^{-2}/\text{Hz}]\times\lvert W\rvert^2\,[\text{s}^2]\times df\,[\text{Hz}]=\text{rad}^2Sν​[rad2s−2/Hz]×∣W∣2[s2]×df[Hz]=rad2 ✓.

Kernel (a): TIE — no differencing, kernel =1=1=1​

Take the variance of Step 1's TIEk=−ϕ(kT)/ω0\text{TIE}_k=-\phi(kT)/\omega_0TIEk​=−ϕ(kT)/ω0​ (here we must assume the power of ϕ\phiϕ is finite within the observation band, so we honestly write the band [f1,f2][f_1,f_2][f1​,f2​]):

 σTIE2=1ω02∫f1f2Sϕ(f) df \boxed{\ \sigma_{\text{TIE}}^2=\frac{1}{\omega_0^2}\int_{f_1}^{f_2}S_\phi(f)\,df\ } σTIE2​=ω02​1​∫f1​f2​​Sϕ​(f)df ​

In practice f1f_1f1​ is set by the measurement duration or the PLL loop bandwidth, and f2f_2f2​ by the measurement bandwidth; a TIE number quoted without its band is meaningless. Canonical Example C (−100-100−100 dBc/Hz@1 MHz, integrated over 1–100 MHz) gives σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs; see the Section 8 marker.
  • dimension check: (rad2/Hz)×Hz / (rad/s)2=s2(\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz})\times\text{Hz}\,/\,(\text{rad/s})^2=\text{s}^2(rad2/Hz)×Hz/(rad/s)2=s2 ✓.

Kernel (b): N-period — first-order difference, kernel 4sin⁡2(πfNT)4\sin^2(\pi fNT)4sin2(πfNT)​

Divide the core lemma (τ0=NT\tau_0=NTτ0​=NT) by ω02\omega_0^2ω02​ to convert to time:

 σP2(N)=1ω02∫0∞Sϕ(f) 4sin⁡2(πfNT) df \boxed{\ \sigma_P^2(N)=\frac{1}{\omega_0^2}\int_0^\infty S_\phi(f)\,4\sin^2(\pi fNT)\,df\ } σP2​(N)=ω02​1​∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)4sin2(πfNT)df ​
  • Kernel shape: as f→0f\to0f→0, 4sin⁡2(πfNT)≈(2πfNT)2∝f24\sin^2(\pi fNT)\approx(2\pi fNT)^2\propto f^24sin2(πfNT)≈(2πfNT)2∝f2 (a first-order high-pass; it suppresses the close-in part); the maximum value 4 is reached at f=1/(2NT)f=1/(2NT)f=1/(2NT); beyond that it oscillates between 0 and 4 with period 1/(NT)1/(NT)1/(NT), averaging 2. The larger NNN, the further the kernel's "window" shifts toward low frequency — long-interval differences see slower drift.

Kernel (c): cycle-to-cycle — second-order difference, kernel 16sin⁡4(πfT)16\sin^4(\pi fT)16sin4(πfT)​

Step 2's CkC_kCk​ is "a first-order difference differenced once more"; the filter is two first-order differences in cascade:

Hc2c(f)=(e−j2πfT−1)2⟹∣Hc2c(f)∣2=∣e−j2πfT−1∣4=[4sin⁡2(πfT)]2=16sin⁡4(πfT),H_{c2c}(f)=\big(e^{-j2\pi fT}-1\big)^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lvert H_{c2c}(f)\rvert^2=\big\lvert e^{-j2\pi fT}-1\big\rvert^4=\big[4\sin^2(\pi fT)\big]^2=16\sin^4(\pi fT),Hc2c​(f)=(e−j2πfT−1)2⟹∣Hc2c​(f)∣2=​e−j2πfT−1​4=[4sin2(πfT)]2=16sin4(πfT),  σc2c2=1ω02∫0∞Sϕ(f) 16sin⁡4(πfT) df \boxed{\ \sigma_{c2c}^2=\frac{1}{\omega_0^2}\int_0^\infty S_\phi(f)\,16\sin^4(\pi fT)\,df\ } σc2c2​=ω02​1​∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)16sin4(πfT)df ​
  • Kernel shape: as f→0f\to0f→0 it behaves like (2πfT)4∝f4(2\pi fT)^4\propto f^4(2πfT)4∝f4 (a second-order high-pass — the least sensitive to close-in noise); the peak of 16 sits at f=1/(2T)=f0/2f=1/(2T)=f_0/2f=1/(2T)=f0​/2, and the oscillation average is 6.
  • Where 16 comes from: 424^242. Each differencing contributes one factor 4 (each containing one 2 from the "variance of a difference" and one 2 from the half-angle identity); squaring gives 16. Every 2 is accounted for by name.

Step 4: white-FM closed form — exact interlock with [P2] Eq.(8)/(11)/(12) (this page's punchline)​

4.1 One standard integral we need (no skipped steps)​

First evaluate ∫0∞1−cos⁡(bx)x2dx\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{1-\cos(bx)}{x^2}dx∫0∞​x21−cos(bx)​dx (b>0b\gt0b>0). Integrate by parts (u=1−cos⁡bxu=1-\cos bxu=1−cosbx, dv=x−2dxdv=x^{-2}dxdv=x−2dx, v=−1/xv=-1/xv=−1/x):

∫0∞1−cos⁡bxx2dx=[−1−cos⁡bxx]0∞⏟=0 (both ends 0)+ b∫0∞sin⁡bxxdx=b⋅π2,\int_0^\infty\frac{1-\cos bx}{x^2}dx =\underbrace{\Big[-\frac{1-\cos bx}{x}\Big]_0^\infty}_{=0\ (\text{both ends }0)} +\,b\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin bx}{x}dx =b\cdot\frac{\pi}{2},∫0∞​x21−cosbx​dx==0 (both ends 0)[−x1−cosbx​]0∞​​​+b∫0∞​xsinbx​dx=b⋅2π​,

where the last step uses the Dirichlet integral ∫0∞sin⁡xxdx=π2\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin x}{x}dx=\frac{\pi}{2}∫0∞​xsinx​dx=2π​ (a standard result). Boundary terms: as x→0x\to0x→0, 1−cos⁡bx≈b2x2/21-\cos bx\approx b^2x^2/21−cosbx≈b2x2/2, so the ratio →0\to0→0; as x→∞x\to\inftyx→∞ the numerator is bounded and 1/x→01/x\to01/x→0 ✓. From sin⁡2(ax)=12[1−cos⁡(2ax)]\sin^2(ax)=\tfrac12\big[1-\cos(2ax)\big]sin2(ax)=21​[1−cos(2ax)] we get

∫0∞sin⁡2(ax)x2dx=12⋅π(2a)2=πa2,∫0∞sin⁡4(ax)x2dx=πa4,\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin^2(ax)}{x^2}dx=\frac12\cdot\frac{\pi(2a)}{2}=\frac{\pi a}{2}, \qquad \int_0^\infty\frac{\sin^4(ax)}{x^2}dx=\frac{\pi a}{4},∫0∞​x2sin2(ax)​dx=21​⋅2π(2a)​=2πa​,∫0∞​x2sin4(ax)​dx=4πa​,

where the second identity uses sin⁡4u=18[4(1−cos⁡2u)−(1−cos⁡4u)]\sin^4 u=\tfrac18\big[4(1-\cos2u)-(1-\cos4u)\big]sin4u=81​[4(1−cos2u)−(1−cos4u)] (obtained by reducing the power of cos⁡2\cos^2cos2 once more): 18[4⋅π(2a)2−π(4a)2]=18(4πa−2πa)=πa4\tfrac18\big[4\cdot\tfrac{\pi(2a)}{2}-\tfrac{\pi(4a)}{2}\big]=\tfrac18(4\pi a-2\pi a)=\tfrac{\pi a}{4}81​[4⋅2π(2a)​−2π(4a)​]=81​(4πa−2πa)=4πa​ ✓.

A white noise current (one-sided PSD SiS_iSi​, A2/Hz\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}A2/Hz) is ISF-weighted and integrated into phase ([P1] Eq.(11), p.182):

ϕ(t)=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ.\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau .ϕ(t)=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ.

The white-noise autocorrelation for a one-sided PSD SiS_iSi​ is Ri(τ)=Si2δ(τ)R_i(\tau)=\tfrac{S_i}{2}\delta(\tau)Ri​(τ)=2Si​​δ(τ) (two-sided flat level Si/2S_i/2Si​/2; this 12\tfrac1221​ is one-sided↔two-sided bookkeeping, see stochastic_noise_basics). The variance of the phase increment over Δt\Delta tΔt (when Δt\Delta tΔt is an integer number of periods, ∫Γ2\int\Gamma^2∫Γ2 equals Γrms2Δt\Gamma_{rms}^2\Delta tΓrms2​Δt exactly):

Var⁡[Δϕ(Δt)]=1qmax2⋅Si2∫tt+ΔtΓ2(ω0τ) dτ=Γrms2qmax2⋅Si2⏟≡ κ2 Δt.\operatorname{Var}\big[\Delta\phi(\Delta t)\big] =\frac{1}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_i}{2}\int_t^{t+\Delta t}\Gamma^2(\omega_0\tau)\,d\tau =\underbrace{\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_i}{2}}_{\equiv\ \kappa^2}\ \Delta t .Var[Δϕ(Δt)]=qmax2​1​⋅2Si​​∫tt+Δt​Γ2(ω0​τ)dτ=≡ κ2qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅2Si​​​​ Δt.  σΔϕ=κΔt,κ=Γrmsqmax12⋅in2‾Δf ([P2] Eq.(8), p.792; Eq.(11)/(12), p.793, verified)\boxed{\ \sigma_{\Delta\phi}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t},\qquad \kappa=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}}{q_{max}}\sqrt{\frac12\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}}\ } \qquad(\text{[P2] Eq.(8), p.792; Eq.(11)/(12), p.793, verified}) σΔϕ​=κΔt​,κ=qmax​Γrms​​21​⋅Δfin2​​​​ ​([P2] Eq.(8), p.792; Eq.(11)/(12), p.793, verified)

There is no ω0\omega_0ω0​ inside it. The two versions differ by a factor ω0\omega_0ω0​; mixing them up costs 10 orders of magnitude — always check the units first.

Sϕ(f)=Γrms2qmax2⋅Si(2πf)2=2κ2(2πf)2[rad2/Hz],S_\phi(f)=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_i}{(2\pi f)^2}=\frac{2\kappa^2}{(2\pi f)^2} \qquad[\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}],Sϕ​(f)=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅(2πf)2Si​​=(2πf)22κ2​[rad2/Hz],

where the 2 here is the standard correspondence "random walk Var⁡=κ2t\operatorname{Var}=\kappa^2 tVar=κ2t ↔ one-sided spectrum 2κ2/Δω22\kappa^2/\Delta\omega^22κ2/Δω2" (two-sided flat level κ2\kappa^2κ2, times 2 for one-sided). Mapping to SSB: the time-domain /2/2/2 convention L=12Sϕ=κ2/Δω2\mathcal{L}=\tfrac12S_\phi=\kappa^2/\Delta\omega^2L=21​Sϕ​=κ2/Δω2 gives −145.0-145.0−145.0 dBc/Hz@1 MHz, while the /4/4/4 convention of [P1] Eq.(21), p.185 gives −148.0-148.0−148.0 dBc/Hz (canonical Example B; lab_24 prints both, see the Section 8 marker).

σP(N)=κNTω0,σP(1)=κTω0.\sigma_P(N)=\frac{\kappa\sqrt{NT}}{\omega_0},\qquad \sigma_P(1)=\frac{\kappa\sqrt{T}}{\omega_0}.σP​(N)=ω0​κNT​​,σP​(1)=ω0​κT​​.

4.4 The cycle-to-cycle closed form and the 2\sqrt22​ relation​

Insert the same SϕS_\phiSϕ​ into kernel (c), using 4.1's ∫sin⁡4(ax)/x2 dx=πa/4\int\sin^4(ax)/x^2\,dx=\pi a/4∫sin4(ax)/x2dx=πa/4 (a=πTa=\pi Ta=πT):

σc2c,ϕ2=2κ2π2⋅4∫0∞sin⁡4(πTf)f2df=8κ2π2⋅π2T4=2κ2T⟹ σc2c=2 σP(1) \sigma_{c2c,\phi}^2=\frac{2\kappa^2}{\pi^2}\cdot4\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin^4(\pi Tf)}{f^2}df =\frac{8\kappa^2}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{\pi^2T}{4}=2\kappa^2T \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{\ \sigma_{c2c}=\sqrt2\,\sigma_P(1)\ }σc2c,ϕ2​=π22κ2​⋅4∫0∞​f2sin4(πTf)​df=π28κ2​⋅4π2T​=2κ2T⟹ σc2c​=2​σP​(1) ​

Physical meaning: under white FM, the length deviations of two adjacent periods are independent (non-overlapping random-walk increments); variances of independent differences add, hence exactly 2\sqrt22​. This is the same statement as [P2] p.803's Eq.(51), which derives the rms cycle-to-cycle jitter "based on (8)" (and is likewise restricted there to phase noise in the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region). If the spectrum is not pure 1/f21/f^21/f2 (e.g., flicker-dominated), adjacent periods are correlated and the 2\sqrt22​ fails — a quick health check of whether a measurement sits in the white-noise region.

4.5 Practical corollary: read κ\kappaκ off L\mathcal{L}L in one step (mind which convention's L\mathcal{L}L)​

In the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region, under the time-domain /2/2/2 convention Llin(Δf)=κ2/(2πΔf)2\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}(\Delta f)=\kappa^2/(2\pi\Delta f)^2Llin​(Δf)=κ2/(2πΔf)2; solving:

κ=2π ΔfLlin(Δf)[rad/s],κω0=Δff0Llin(Δf)[s].\kappa=2\pi\,\Delta f\sqrt{\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}(\Delta f)}\quad[\text{rad}/\sqrt{\text{s}}], \qquad \frac{\kappa}{\omega_0}=\frac{\Delta f}{f_0}\sqrt{\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}(\Delta f)}\quad[\sqrt{\text{s}}].κ=2πΔfLlin​(Δf)​[rad/s​],ω0​κ​=f0​Δf​Llin​(Δf)​[s​].

This corresponds to [P2] Eq.(50), p.803 (the white-noise special case: read κ\kappaκ off the L\mathcal{L}L of the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region; the literal original equation is transcribed verbatim in the v5 verification note above). Factor-of-2 trap: this formula takes numbers in the L=12Sϕ\mathcal{L}=\tfrac12S_\phiL=21​Sϕ​ (time-domain /2/2/2) convention — for the canonical oscillator, plugging in −145-145−145 dBc/Hz gives κ=0.354\kappa=0.354κ=0.354 ✓; mistakenly plugging in the −148-148−148 of [P1] Eq.(21)'s /4/4/4 convention loses a 2\sqrt22​ (gives 0.25). Same oscillator, same spectrum — first ask which bookkeeping the dBc/Hz number uses, then plug it into the formula.

Paper-native derivation: [P2] Appendix A (the paper's own source for Eq.(11), transcribed verbatim and reconciled factor by factor)​

Steps 3 and 4 are this site's own derivation; [P2] actually walks the very same ground twice, once along each route, in Appendix A "Relationship Between Jitter and Phase Noise" — it starts in the right column of p.802 and ends in the left column of p.803 (the right column of p.803 onward is Appendix B on nonsymmetric edges; don't confuse the two): Eq.(40)–(44) is the white-noise time-domain route (= Section 4.2 of this page), Eq.(45)–(49) is the autocorrelation + Khinchin route (= this page's Route A), followed by two practical corollaries Eq.(50)/(51) (= Section 4.5 and the one-period version of 4.4). The main text on p.793 states explicitly that Eq.(11)'s source is here ("As shown in Appendix A, for ΔT≫T\Delta T\gg TΔT≫T or ΔT=nT\Delta T=nTΔT=nT…", immediately followed by σΔϕ2=Γrms2⋅in2‾/Δf2qmax2ΔT\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2\cdot\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{2q_{max}^2}\Delta TσΔϕ2​=2qmax2​Γrms2​⋅in2​​/Δf​ΔT). What follows is transcribed verbatim from the rendered PDF pages of p.802–803 (verified under magnification), exactly as printed — printing slips included.

A.1 The white-noise time-domain route: Eq.(40)–(44) (p.802, right column)​

The definition of phase jitter (in the paper's words: "The phase jitter is"):

σΔϕ2=E{Δϕ2}=E{[ϕ(t+ΔT)−ϕ(t)]2}([P2] Eq.(40), p.802)\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2=E\{\Delta\phi^2\}=E\big\{[\phi(t+\Delta T)-\phi(t)]^2\big\} \qquad(\text{[P2] Eq.(40), p.802})σΔϕ2​=E{Δϕ2}=E{[ϕ(t+ΔT)−ϕ(t)]2}([P2] Eq.(40), p.802)

where (the ISF phase integral of [P1], with its limits cut to the observation window):

Δϕ=∫0ΔTΓ(ω0τ)qmax i(τ) dτ.(Eq.(41))\Delta\phi=\int_0^{\Delta T}\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,i(\tau)\,d\tau. \qquad(\text{Eq.(41)})Δϕ=∫0ΔT​qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​i(τ)dτ.(Eq.(41))

Squaring and exchanging expectation with integration:

σΔϕ2=1qmax2∫0ΔT ⁣ ⁣∫0ΔTΓ(ω0τ1) Γ(ω0τ2)⋅E[i(τ1)i(τ2)] dτ1 dτ2.(Eq.(42))\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2=\frac{1}{q_{max}^2}\int_0^{\Delta T}\!\!\int_0^{\Delta T} \Gamma(\omega_0\tau_1)\,\Gamma(\omega_0\tau_2)\cdot E[i(\tau_1)i(\tau_2)]\,d\tau_1\,d\tau_2. \qquad(\text{Eq.(42)})σΔϕ2​=qmax2​1​∫0ΔT​∫0ΔT​Γ(ω0​τ1​)Γ(ω0​τ2​)⋅E[i(τ1​)i(τ2​)]dτ1​dτ2​.(Eq.(42))

The paper writes the white-noise current autocorrelation explicitly as Rii(t1,t2)=(1/2)(in2‾/Δf)δ(t1−t2)R_{ii}(t_1,t_2)=(1/2)\big(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f\big)\delta(t_1-t_2)Rii​(t1​,t2​)=(1/2)(in2​​/Δf)δ(t1​−t2​); substituting it collapses the double integral into a single one:

σΔϕ2=12 in2‾/Δfqmax2∫0ΔTΓ2(ω0τ) dτ(Eq.(43))\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2=\frac12\,\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{q_{max}^2} \int_0^{\Delta T}\Gamma^2(\omega_0\tau)\,d\tau \qquad(\text{Eq.(43)})σΔϕ2​=21​qmax2​in2​​/Δf​∫0ΔT​Γ2(ω0​τ)dτ(Eq.(43)) σΔϕ2=12 in2‾/Δfqmax2 Γrms2 ΔTforΔT≫T or ΔT=mT.(Eq.(44))\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2=\frac12\,\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{q_{max}^2}\, \Gamma_{rms}^2\,\Delta T \quad\text{for}\quad\Delta T\gg T\ \text{or}\ \Delta T=mT. \qquad(\text{Eq.(44)})σΔϕ2​=21​qmax2​in2​​/Δf​Γrms2​ΔTforΔT≫T or ΔT=mT.(Eq.(44))

Eq.(44) is literally the main text's Eq.(11) (p.793; only the typesetting differs), and its coefficient 12 (in2‾/Δf) Γrms2/qmax2\tfrac12\,(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)\,\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^221​(in2​​/Δf)Γrms2​/qmax2​ is exactly the κ2\kappa^2κ2 of Section 4.2 (with Si≡in2‾/ΔfS_i\equiv\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fSi​≡in2​​/Δf) — the paper's time-domain route matches 4.2 symbol for symbol.

A.2 The autocorrelation + Khinchin route: Eq.(45)–(51) (p.803, left column)​

The paper then switches to the second route — stating up front that timing jitter is the standard deviation of the timing uncertainty:

plus the two practical corollaries restricted to white noise (the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region) — Eq.(50) is obtained by combining the main text's (6)+(12), and Eq.(51) then follows "based on (8)" (i.e., σ=κT\sigma=\kappa\sqrt Tσ=κT​); neither comes from integrating (49):

As-printed disclosure (verified under magnification; symbol overloading and printing slips listed honestly):

  1. σΔϕ2\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2σΔϕ2​ does double duty: in Eq.(40)–(44) the LHS is phase jitter (rad²); from Eq.(45) on, the LHS is still printed σΔϕ2\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2σΔϕ2​ yet carries an extra 1/ω021/\omega_0^21/ω02​, and the text explicitly calls it timing jitter — it is really σΔT2=σΔϕ2/ω02\sigma_{\Delta T}^2=\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2/\omega_0^2σΔT2​=σΔϕ2​/ω02​ (s², i.e., the Eq.(10) conversion). This page names σΔϕ\sigma_{\Delta\phi}σΔϕ​ and σΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}σΔt​ separately precisely to defuse this mine.
  2. The expansion line of Eq.(45) drops two symbols: the middle term is missing its EEE, and the cross term is missing its factor 2 (the cross term of [a−b]2[a-b]^2[a−b]2 is 2ab2ab2ab; under stationarity the first two terms combine into 2Rϕ(0)2R_\phi(0)2Rϕ​(0), so landing on Eq.(47) requires the cross term to be 2Rϕ(ΔT)2R_\phi(\Delta T)2Rϕ​(ΔT)). Eq.(47) itself is printed correctly — the slip does not propagate.
  3. τ\tauτ and ΔT\Delta TΔT are mixed: Eq.(46) writes Rϕ(τ)R_\phi(\tau)Rϕ​(τ) on the LHS but uses ΔT\Delta TΔT on the RHS; the kernel of Eq.(49) is written sin⁡2(πfτ)\sin^2(\pi f\tau)sin2(πfτ), where this τ\tauτ is the delay ΔT\Delta TΔT.

The numerator of Eq.(51) is printed as fff: multiplying Eq.(50)'s (time-version) κ\kappaκ by T=f0−0.5\sqrt T=f_0^{-0.5}T​=f0−0.5​ gives σCTC=κT\sigma_{CTC}=\kappa\sqrt TσCTC​=κT​, so the numerator should be the offset frequency Δf\Delta fΔf — the printing swallowed the Δ\DeltaΔ (the transcription in "Corresponding papers / equations" is annotated accordingly).
  5. The integration limits ∫−∞∞\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}∫−∞∞​ of Eq.(48) declare that SϕS_\phiSϕ​ here is a two-sided spectrum — the only place in the whole paper where the convention leaks out; the 8 of Eq.(49) therefore has one bookkeeping 2 built in (see the table below).

A.4 Who skips what (honest bookkeeping in both directions)​

Skipped by [P2], filled in by this page:

  • The stationarity rigor gap: Eq.(45)–(47) needs Rϕ(0)R_\phi(0)Rϕ​(0) finite; a free-running oscillator's ϕ\phiϕ is a random walk, so Rϕ(0)R_\phi(0)Rϕ​(0) diverges (exactly the confession at the start of this page's Route A). The difference Rϕ(0)−Rϕ(ΔT)R_\phi(0)-R_\phi(\Delta T)Rϕ​(0)−Rϕ​(ΔT) is finite and the conclusion survives, but making it rigorous requires this page's Route B (which only demands that ν=ϕ˙\nu=\dot\phiν=ϕ˙​ be stationary) — the paper does not address this step.
  • No convention declared: not one sentence in the paper says whether SϕS_\phiSϕ​ is one- or two-sided; only the integration limits of Eq.(48) give it away. This page's three-column table in Step 0 lays that out in the open (v5 used exactly those limits to infer "two-sided" and reconcile the literature's "coefficient-8 version" with the one-sided 4sin⁡24\sin^24sin2 kernel).
  • The two routes are never interlocked in the paper: Eq.(44) stops in the time domain, Eq.(49) stops in the frequency domain; the paper never substitutes the white-noise spectrum into (49) to check that it lands back on (44). This page's 4.1 integral ∫0∞sin⁡2(ax)/x2 dx=πa/2\int_0^\infty\sin^2(ax)/x^2\,dx=\pi a/2∫0∞​sin2(ax)/x2dx=πa/2 plus the substitution in 4.3 is that missing closed loop (the code below computes both routes — same number).
  • Neither the time-domain flicker 1/f31/f^31/f3 closed form (Step 5's log formula) nor the c2c 16sin⁡416\sin^416sin4 kernel (kernel (c); Eq.(51) is only the one-period version) appears in the paper.

Glossed over by this page, written out in full by [P2]:

  • The general double integral of Eq.(42): Section 4.2 jumps straight to "white-noise δ correlation ⇒ single integral"; the paper writes out the general form Γ(ω0τ1)Γ(ω0τ2) E[i(τ1)i(τ2)]\Gamma(\omega_0\tau_1)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau_2)\,E[i(\tau_1)i(\tau_2)]Γ(ω0​τ1​)Γ(ω0​τ2​)E[i(τ1​)i(τ2​)] — the starting point that accepts any colored-noise autocorrelation, with white noise merely a special case.
  • The validity condition printed inside the equation: Eq.(44)'s "for ΔT≫T\Delta T\gg TΔT≫T or ΔT=mT\Delta T=mTΔT=mT" prints right next to the equals sign the condition for ∫Γ2→Γrms2ΔT\int\Gamma^2\to\Gamma_{rms}^2\Delta T∫Γ2→Γrms2​ΔT to be exact; this page's 4.2 only mentions it in a parenthesis. For short or non-integer ΔT\Delta TΔT there is an O(T/ΔT)O(T/\Delta T)O(T/ΔT)-level Γ2\Gamma^2Γ2 ripple residual.

A.5 Replaying the white-FM variance along both routes (checkable via # ->)​

import numpy as np
from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal

F0, T = 5e9, 2e-10
W0 = 2 * np.pi * F0
QMAX, SI, GRMS = 1e-12, 1e-24, 0.5      # canonical parameters
N = 100
DT = N * T                              # ΔT = mT (the validity condition of Eq.(44))

# Route 1: [P2] Appendix A time-domain autocorrelation route —
# substituting R_ii=(S_i/2)δ into Eq.(42) collapses it to Eq.(43)
tau = np.linspace(0.0, DT, 200 * N + 1)
gam = np.sqrt(2.0) * GRMS * gamma_lc_ideal(W0 * tau)     # LC-shaped ISF with Γrms=0.5
var_43 = 0.5 * SI / QMAX**2 * np.trapezoid(gam**2, tau)  # Eq.(43), numerical integral
var_44 = 0.5 * SI / QMAX**2 * GRMS**2 * DT               # Eq.(44) = main text Eq.(11)
print(f"{var_43:.4e}")            # -> 2.5000e-09 rad^2 (Eq.(43), σ²_Δφ @ N=100)
print(f"{var_43/var_44:.4f}")     # -> 1.0000 (at ΔT=mT, ∫Γ² is exactly Γrms²ΔT)

# Route 2: this page's kernel route — one-sided S_φ=2κ²/(2πf)² times the 4sin²(πfΔT) kernel
kappa2 = GRMS**2 / QMAX**2 * SI / 2                      # κ²=Γrms²S_i/(2q_max²)
print(f"{kappa2:.4f}")            # -> 0.1250 rad^2/s (the same prefactor as Eq.(44))
x = np.linspace(1e-8, 1e4, 4_000_001)                    # x = fΔT
core = np.trapezoid(np.sin(np.pi * x)**2 / x**2, x) + 0.5 / x[-1]  # tail: sin²→1/2
var_kernel = 2 * kappa2 * DT / np.pi**2 * core           # = κ²ΔT (the 4.3 analytic value)
print(f"{var_kernel/var_43:.4f}") # -> 1.0000 (frequency kernel = Appendix A route, same number)

# Reconciling [P2] Eq.(49): 8/ω₀² × two-sided S_φ^DS=κ²/(2πf)², LHS is the time-version variance
var_49 = 8 / W0**2 * (kappa2 * DT / 4 / np.pi**2) * core
print(f"{var_49/(kappa2*DT/W0**2):.4f}")   # -> 1.0000 (8 = 2(two-sided→one-sided)×4(kernel))
print(f"{np.sqrt(var_49)*1e15:.2f} fs")    # -> 1.59 fs (σ_ΔT @ N=100 = √100×0.159 fs)

The first two prints walk [P2] Eq.(43)→(44) (the time-domain autocorrelation route); the remaining four walk this page's kernel (b) and the two-sided bookkeeping of Eq.(49) — one oscillator, two routes, one number, κ2ΔT=2.5×10−9 rad2\kappa^2\Delta T=2.5\times10^{-9}\ \text{rad}^2κ2ΔT=2.5×10−9 rad2. Appendix A and Steps 3/4 of this page are two proofs of the same theorem; the only difference is that the paper hides its convention inside the integration limits, while this page prints it in Step 0.

Step 5: the flicker (1/f31/f^31/f3) closed form — the log term and its honesty conditions​

Flicker FM has the phase spectrum Sϕ(f)=b3/f3S_\phi(f)=b_3/f^3Sϕ​(f)=b3​/f3 (b3b_3b3​ in rad2⋅Hz2\text{rad}^2\cdot\text{Hz}^2rad2⋅Hz2; for its origin see flicker_noise_upconversion). The kernel-(b) integral behaves at f→0f\to0f→0 as ∫(b3/f3)(2πfNT)2df∝∫df/f\int(b_3/f^3)(2\pi fNT)^2df\propto\int df/f∫(b3​/f3)(2πfNT)2df∝∫df/f — logarithmically divergent — so a low-frequency cutoff flf_lfl​ must honestly be introduced (physically: a measurement of duration TobsT_{obs}Tobs​ gives fl∼1/Tobsf_l\sim1/T_{obs}fl​∼1/Tobs​, or the PLL pins everything below). What we compute is

σΔϕ2(N)=4b3∫fl∞sin⁡2(af)f3 df,a=πNT.\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2(N)=4b_3\int_{f_l}^{\infty}\frac{\sin^2(af)}{f^3}\,df,\qquad a=\pi NT .σΔϕ2​(N)=4b3​∫fl​∞​f3sin2(af)​df,a=πNT.

Step 1 (half-angle): sin⁡2(af)=12[1−cos⁡(2af)]\sin^2(af)=\tfrac12[1-\cos(2af)]sin2(af)=21​[1−cos(2af)]; write b=2ab=2ab=2a and J(b,fl)=∫fl∞1−cos⁡(bf)f3dfJ(b,f_l)=\int_{f_l}^\infty\frac{1-\cos(bf)}{f^3}dfJ(b,fl​)=∫fl​∞​f31−cos(bf)​df, so the integral =12J=\tfrac12 J=21​J.

Step 2 (integrate by parts once, v=−1/(2f2)v=-1/(2f^2)v=−1/(2f2)):

J=1−cos⁡(bfl)2fl2+b2∫fl∞sin⁡(bf)f2 df.J=\frac{1-\cos(bf_l)}{2f_l^2}+\frac{b}{2}\int_{f_l}^\infty\frac{\sin(bf)}{f^2}\,df .J=2fl2​1−cos(bfl​)​+2b​∫fl​∞​f2sin(bf)​df.

Step 3 (integrate by parts again, v=−1/fv=-1/fv=−1/f):

∫fl∞sin⁡(bf)f2df=sin⁡(bfl)fl+b∫fl∞cos⁡(bf)fdf=sin⁡(bfl)fl−b Ci(bfl),\int_{f_l}^\infty\frac{\sin(bf)}{f^2}df=\frac{\sin(bf_l)}{f_l}+b\int_{f_l}^\infty\frac{\cos(bf)}{f}df =\frac{\sin(bf_l)}{f_l}-b\,\mathrm{Ci}(bf_l),∫fl​∞​f2sin(bf)​df=fl​sin(bfl​)​+b∫fl​∞​fcos(bf)​df=fl​sin(bfl​)​−bCi(bfl​),

where Ci(z)=−∫z∞cos⁡uudu\mathrm{Ci}(z)=-\int_z^\infty\frac{\cos u}{u}duCi(z)=−∫z∞​ucosu​du is the cosine integral function.

Example: b3=1 rad2Hz2b_3=1\ \text{rad}^2\text{Hz}^2b3​=1 rad2Hz2, fl=100f_l=100fl​=100 Hz, N=1N=1N=1, T=200T=200T=200 ps: 2πNTfl=1.26×10−72\pi NTf_l=1.26\times10^{-7}2πNTfl​=1.26×10−7, bracket =0.9228+15.89=16.81=0.9228+15.89=16.81=0.9228+15.89=16.81, σΔϕ2=1.579×10−18×16.81=2.65×10−17 rad2\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2=1.579\times10^{-18}\times16.81=2.65\times10^{-17}\ \text{rad}^2σΔϕ2​=1.579×10−18×16.81=2.65×10−17 rad2. Changing flf_lfl​ by 10× only shifts the bracket to 16.81∓2.3016.81\mp2.3016.81∓2.30 (∓14%\mp14\%∓14% in variance) — the log's sluggishness is good news, but it is not zero.
  • Growth law in NNN: σΔϕ(N)∝Nln⁡(⋅)\sigma_{\Delta\phi}(N)\propto N\sqrt{\ln(\cdot)}σΔϕ​(N)∝Nln(⋅)​ — almost linear (lab_24 prints σ(N=10)/σ(N=1)=9.29\sigma(N{=}10)/\sigma(N{=}1)=9.29σ(N=10)/σ(N=1)=9.29; white FM would give 10=3.16\sqrt{10}=3.1610​=3.16). Solid-State Circuits, vol. 32, no. 6, pp. 870–879, Jun. 1997 (external literature, not among the 5 source PDFs).

Step 5b: two-regime growth — [P2] Fig.16's σ(Δt)=κ2Δt+ζ2Δt2\sigma(\Delta t)=\sqrt{\kappa^2\Delta t+\zeta^2\Delta t^2}σ(Δt)=κ2Δt+ζ2Δt2​​

Step 4 (white FM: σ2=κ2Δt\sigma^2=\kappa^2\Delta tσ2=κ2Δt, slope 1/2) and Step 5 (flicker FM: σ2∼ζ2Δt2\sigma^2\sim\zeta^2\Delta t^2σ2∼ζ2Δt2, slope ≈1\approx1≈1) coexist in every real oscillator. [P2] literally measures this for you — that is the famous two-regime log-log plot of Fig. 16.

5b.1 [P2] verbatim (verified against the rendered PDF pages)​

  • Fig. 16 caption (p.802): "RMS jitter versus measurement interval for the four-stage, 2.8-GHz differential ring oscillator (oscillator number 12)." The vertical axis reads "Rms jitter (second)", the horizontal axis "ΔT\Delta TΔT (second)"; the two asymptote fits on the plot are annotated κ=6.18e-9 sec0.5\kappa=6.18\text{e-}9\ \text{sec}^{0.5}κ=6.18e-9 sec0.5 and ζ=2.5e5\zeta=2.5\text{e}5ζ=2.5e5.
  • Definitions of the two proportionality constants (p.792): Eq.(8) σΔT=κΔT\sigma_{\Delta T}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta T}σΔT​=κΔT​, "where κ\kappaκ is a proportionality constant determined by circuit parameters"; Eq.(9) σΔT=ζ ΔT\sigma_{\Delta T}=\zeta\,\Delta TσΔT​=ζΔT, "where ζ\zetaζ is another proportionality constant". The premise of Eq.(9) is fully correlated noise sources — in the paper's words: "when the noise sources are totally correlated with one another … the standard deviations rather than the variances add"; substrate/supply noise and low-frequency 1/f noise belong to this class. Same page, the conclusion: "a log–log plot of the timing jitter σΔT\sigma_{\Delta T}σΔT​ versus the measurement delay ΔT\Delta TΔT for an open-loop oscillator will demonstrate regions with slopes of 1/2 and 1, as shown in Fig. 4."
  • Measurement cross-check (p.801): "The best fit κ\kappaκ for the data shown in Fig. 16 is κ=6.18×10−9s\kappa=6.18\times10^{-9}\sqrt{s}κ=6.18×10−9s​. Equations (12) and (35) result in κ=5.95×10−9s\kappa=5.95\times10^{-9}\sqrt{s}κ=5.95×10−9s​ and κ=6.07×10−9s\kappa=6.07\times10^{-9}\sqrt{s}κ=6.07×10−9s​, respectively." — ISF theory lands within 2–4% of measurement, one of the most beautiful closed loops in all of [P2]. The slope-1 attribution is on the same page: "The region of the jitter plot with the slope of one can be attributed to the 1/f1/f1/f noise of the devices, as discussed at the end of Section VI." (End of Section VI, pp.797–798: "Low-frequency noise can also result in correlation between uncertainties introduced during different cycles … the uncertainties add up in amplitude rather than power, resulting in a region with a slope of one … even in the absence of external noise sources".)
  • Printing erratum (honesty note): the figure prints ζ\zetaζ as "2.5e5". But Eq.(9) σ=ζΔT\sigma=\zeta\Delta Tσ=ζΔT (seconds =ζ×=\zeta\times=ζ× seconds) makes ζ\zetaζ dimensionless, and the slope-1 fit line passes through (10−610^{-6}10−6 s, ≈2×10−11\approx2\times10^{-11}≈2×10−11 s), so ζ=σ/ΔT≈2.5×10−5\zeta=\sigma/\Delta T\approx2.5\times10^{-5}ζ=σ/ΔT≈2.5×10−5 — the printed exponent is missing its minus sign. This page uses ζ=2.5×10−5\zeta=2.5\times10^{-5}ζ=2.5×10−5 throughout. (Incidental dimension check: κ\kappaκ is annotated sec0.5\text{sec}^{0.5}sec0.5 ✓, s/s=s\text{s}/\sqrt{\text{s}}=\sqrt{\text{s}}s/s​=s​.)

5b.2 Composing the two: independent ⇒ variances add​

White FM (device thermal noise) and flicker FM (device 1/f) come from distinct physical mechanisms and are statistically independent; the variance of a sum of independent random variables is the sum of the variances (the cross term has zero expectation):

σΔt2(Δt)=κ2 Δt⏟Step 4 (white)+ζ2 Δt2⏟Step 5 (flicker)\sigma_{\Delta t}^2(\Delta t)=\underbrace{\kappa^2\,\Delta t}_{\text{Step 4 (white)}}+\underbrace{\zeta^2\,\Delta t^2}_{\text{Step 5 (flicker)}}σΔt2​(Δt)=Step 4 (white)κ2Δt​​+Step 5 (flicker)ζ2Δt2​​  σΔt(Δt)=κ2 Δt+ζ2 Δt2 \boxed{\ \sigma_{\Delta t}(\Delta t)=\sqrt{\kappa^2\,\Delta t+\zeta^2\,\Delta t^2}\ } σΔt​(Δt)=κ2Δt+ζ2Δt2​ ​
  • Honesty note on provenance: this composed formula does not appear verbatim in [P2] — the paper gives the two limiting behaviors Eq.(8)/(9) and the two-segment plots of Fig.4/Fig.16; adding in quadrature is the direct corollary of "independent ⇒ variances add" ([P2] p.792 says "standard deviations add" for correlated sources and variances add for independent ones; between the two noise classes, white and 1/f, it is the latter).
  • Units (time version): the κ,ζ\kappa,\zetaκ,ζ of this section are the time versions — [κ]=s[\kappa]=\sqrt{\text{s}}[κ]=s​ (κ2Δt: s⋅s=s2\kappa^2\Delta t:\ \text{s}\cdot\text{s}=\text{s}^2κ2Δt: s⋅s=s2 ✓), ζ\zetaζ dimensionless (ζ2Δt2=s2\zeta^2\Delta t^2=\text{s}^2ζ2Δt2=s2 ✓). The phase versions (rad bookkeeping) carry an extra ω0\omega_0ω0​ each: κϕ=ω0κ\kappa_\phi=\omega_0\kappaκϕ​=ω0​κ (Section 4.2), ζϕ=ω0ζ\zeta_\phi=\omega_0\zetaζϕ​=ω0​ζ ([ζϕ]=rad/s[\zeta_\phi]=\text{rad/s}[ζϕ​]=rad/s).
  • The corner: set the two terms equal, ␀κ2Δtc=ζ2Δtc2\kappa^2\Delta t_c=\zeta^2\Delta t_c^2κ2Δtc​=ζ2Δtc2​, and solve:
 Δtc=κ2ζ2 [s1]=s ✓\boxed{\ \Delta t_c=\frac{\kappa^2}{\zeta^2}\ }\qquad \Big[\frac{\text{s}}{1}\Big]=\text{s}\ \checkmark Δtc​=ζ2κ2​ ​[1s​]=s ✓

For Δt≪Δtc\Delta t\ll\Delta t_cΔt≪Δtc​ white noise dominates (slope 1/2); for Δt≫Δtc\Delta t\gg\Delta t_cΔt≫Δtc​ flicker dominates (slope 1); at Δtc\Delta t_cΔtc​ the composed curve sits 2\sqrt22​ (3 dB) above either asymptote — each term contributes half.

5b.3 Reconciling with Step 5's log closed form — "constant ζ\zetaζ" is a slowly-varying approximation​

Step 5's rigorous result (converted to time units, dividing by ω02\omega_0^2ω02​) is

σΔt,flicker2(Δt)=4π2b3ω02 Δt2[32−γ−ln⁡(2πΔt fl)]⟹ζeff2(Δt)=4π2b3ω02[32−γ−ln⁡(2πΔt fl)],\sigma_{\Delta t,\text{flicker}}^2(\Delta t)=\frac{4\pi^2 b_3}{\omega_0^2}\,\Delta t^2\Big[\tfrac32-\gamma-\ln(2\pi\Delta t\,f_l)\Big] \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \zeta_{\rm eff}^2(\Delta t)=\frac{4\pi^2 b_3}{\omega_0^2}\Big[\tfrac32-\gamma-\ln(2\pi\Delta t\,f_l)\Big],σΔt,flicker2​(Δt)=ω02​4π2b3​​Δt2[23​−γ−ln(2πΔtfl​)]⟹ζeff2​(Δt)=ω02​4π2b3​​[23​−γ−ln(2πΔtfl​)],

i.e., ζ\zetaζ is not a constant — it shrinks slowly with Δt\Delta tΔt as log⁡\sqrt{\log}log​ (unit check: b3/ω02=[rad2Hz2]/[rad/s]2=b_3/\omega_0^2=[\text{rad}^2\text{Hz}^2]/[\text{rad/s}]^2=b3​/ω02​=[rad2Hz2]/[rad/s]2= dimensionless ✓). The local log-log slope deviates from 1 accordingly:

dln⁡σdln⁡Δt=1−12[32−γ−ln⁡(2πΔtfl)].\frac{d\ln\sigma}{d\ln\Delta t}=1-\frac{1}{2\big[\tfrac32-\gamma-\ln(2\pi\Delta t f_l)\big]} .dlnΔtdlnσ​=1−2[23​−γ−ln(2πΔtfl​)]1​.
  • The lab_24 Part 5 MC (fl=298f_l=298fl​=298 Hz, set by the simulation length) fits a slope of 0.909 in the flicker region, while the exact curve over the same window gives 0.911 — the MC's deviation from 1.0 is physics (the log correction), not noise.
  • In real measurements flf_lfl​ is set by the measurement duration (seconds ⇒ fl∼1f_l\sim1fl​∼1 Hz), the bracket is ≈13\approx13≈13–161616, and the local slope is 0.9670.9670.967 (Δt=10−7\Delta t=10^{-7}Δt=10−7 s, fl=1f_l=1fl​=1 Hz, printed by lab_24) — which is why [P2] Fig.16 can be fitted with a clean slope-1 straight line: the log correction is invisible over hardware decade spans. The paper's constant ζ\zetaζ is the tangent approximation "bracket frozen at its corner value"; our figure (below) draws both, and they nearly coincide.

5b.4 Time-domain corner ↔ frequency-domain 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner (the honest mapping)​

Define the spectral corner f1/f3≡b3/b2f_{1/f^3}\equiv b_3/b_2f1/f3​≡b3​/b2​ (the offset frequency at which the 1/f31/f^31/f3 and 1/f21/f^21/f2 segments of SϕS_\phiSϕ​ are equal). Because it is a ratio within one and the same spectrum, the SSB /2/2/2 vs /4/4/4 bookkeepings cancel between numerator and denominator — a rare corner of this page where no convention needs minding. Insert Step 4's κϕ2=2π2b2\kappa_\phi^2=2\pi^2b_2κϕ2​=2π2b2​ and the ζeff\zeta_{\rm eff}ζeff​ above into Δtc=κ2/ζ2\Delta t_c=\kappa^2/\zeta^2Δtc​=κ2/ζ2 (the time and phase versions give the same ratio; ω02\omega_0^2ω02​ cancels):

Δtc=2π2b24␀π2b3[⋅]= 12[⋅] f1/f3 ,[⋅]=32−γ−ln⁡(2πΔtcfl) (self-consistent).\Delta t_c=\frac{2\pi^2 b_2}{4\pi^2 b_3\big[\cdot\big]} =\boxed{\ \frac{1}{2\big[\cdot\big]\,f_{1/f^3}}\ },\qquad \big[\cdot\big]=\tfrac32-\gamma-\ln(2\pi\Delta t_c f_l)\ (\text{self-consistent}).Δtc​=4π2b3​[⋅]2π2b2​​= 2[⋅]f1/f3​1​ ​,[⋅]=23​−γ−ln(2πΔtc​fl​) (self-consistent).
  • This 2 is not an SSB bookkeeping 2: the 2 in the denominator is the ratio of the two kernel-integral constants — the white-noise integral ∫sin⁡2(ax)/x2 dx=πa/2\int\sin^2(ax)/x^2\,dx=\pi a/2∫sin2(ax)/x2dx=πa/2 (Section 4.1) against the flicker log form (Step 5) — a convention-free physical constant.
  • Order-of-magnitude intuition: [⋅]≈10[\cdot]\approx10[⋅]≈10–161616, so Δtc\Delta t_cΔtc​ is 20–30× shorter than the naive guess 1/f1/f31/f_{1/f^3}1/f1/f3​. "The spectral corner is at 1 MHz, so the time-domain knee is at 1 µs" is wrong by a decade and a half — the log bracket is the culprit.
  • Not the same thing as [P2] Eq.(57): App. B's f1/f3=f1/f⋅32ηN(1−A)21−A+A2f_{1/f^3}=f_{1/f}\cdot\frac{3}{2\eta N}\frac{(1-A)^2}{1-A+A^2}f1/f3​=f1/f​⋅2ηN3​1−A+A2(1−A)2​ is the circuit-level mapping "device 1/f corner → spectral corner"; this section's f1/f3=b3/b2f_{1/f^3}=b_3/b_2f1/f3​=b3​/b2​ is the observational definition of the spectral corner itself. Same corner, different routes to it.

Part 1 — not an abstract random walk, but the mechanism of [P1] Eq.(11): finely sampled white noise current → ISF weighting → cumulative integration → per-cycle phase increment. Verifies that the increment standard deviation =κT=\kappa\sqrt T=κT​ and that adjacent cycles are uncorrelated:

i_n   = white_noise(n, psd=SI, fs=fs, rng=RNG)          # one-sided PSD = S_i
gamma = np.sqrt(2.0) * GRMS * gamma_lc_ideal(W0 * t)    # rms = 0.5
phi   = np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum(gamma * i_n * dt / QMAX)))
d1    = np.diff(phi[::n_per])                           # per-cycle phase increment
print(f"{rms(d1):.4e}")        # -> 5.0051e-06 rad (theory kappa*sqrt(T)=5.0000e-06)
print(f"{ratio:.3f}")          # -> 1.001
print(f"{corr1:+.4f}")         # -> -0.0012 (adjacent-cycle increments uncorrelated)

Part 2 — measure the three jitters directly in the time domain (a random walk of 2×10⁶ cycles; middle and right columns of the figure):

# N-period phase jitter: rms(phi[N:]-phi[:-N]) vs theory kappa*sqrt(N*T)
# N=1   ratio MC/theory  # -> 0.999
# N=10  ratio            # -> 0.999
# N=100 ratio            # -> 1.001
# period jitter [fs]     # -> 0.1590 fs (theory 0.1592 fs, ratio 0.999)
# cycle-to-cycle [fs]    # -> 0.2248 fs (theory sqrt(2)*sigma_P=0.2251 fs, ratio 0.999)

S_phi = 2 * KAPPA**2 / (2*np.pi*f)**2                   # white-FM one-sided spectrum
num   = trapz(S_phi * 4*np.sin(np.pi*f*N*T)**2, f) + tail

# -> -148.0 dBc/Hz ([P1] Eq.(21) /4 convention)

Part 4 — the canonical Example C spectrum (−100-100−100 dBc/Hz@1 MHz, 1/f21/f^21/f2), tying the site's three numbers together:

sigma_t, sigma_phi = integrate_rms_jitter(fgrid, L, f0=5e9, fmin=1e6, fmax=100e6)
print(f"{sigma_t*1e15:.1f} fs")     # -> 447.9 fs TIE (Example C, lower-limit dominated)
print(f"{np.sqrt(b2*T**3/2)*1e15:.2f} fs")   # -> 28.28 fs period-jitter closed form
print(f"{kappa_c:.2f}")             # -> 62.83 rad/sqrt(s) (=2π·1MHz·√L_lin; κ_C√T/ω0 also = 28.28 fs)

Part 5 — two-regime growth (white + flicker FM composed; corresponds to Step 5b and [P2] Fig.16): both noise classes are synthesized as per-period phase increments — white increments N(0,κ2T)\mathcal{N}(0,\kappa^2T)N(0,κ2T) (justified by Part 1) plus flicker increments (flicker_noise spectral shaping, level calibrated by Welch) — over 2242^{24}224 periods, with σ(Δt)\sigma(\Delta t)σ(Δt) spanning 5 decades:

b2      = KAPPA2 / (2*np.pi**2); b3 = b2 * 1e6        # target f_{1/f^3} = 1 MHz
k_flick = 2*np.pi**2 * b3 * T**2 * fs                 # so that S_d(f) = 4pi^2 b3 T^2 / f
d_fl    = flicker_noise(n_periods, fs=fs, k_flicker=k_flick, rng=RNG)
d_w     = RNG.normal(0.0, KAPPA*np.sqrt(T), n_periods)
phi     = np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum(d_w + d_fl)))
sig_t   = np.array([rms(phi[N:] - phi[:-N]) for N in Ns]) / W0   # [s]
# flicker level calibration S_d*f  # -> 1.000e-14 rad^2 (nominal also 1.000e-14)
# b3 / f_{1/f^3}                   # -> 6.333e+03 rad^2*Hz^2 / 1.000e+06 Hz
# fitted slope, white region (N≤32)     # -> 0.519 (theory 0.5; exact curve over same window 0.520)
# fitted slope, flicker region (N≥3200) # -> 0.909 (clean ζΔt would be 1.0; exact over same window 0.911)
# corner: MC fit-line intersection  # -> 4.31e-08 s (216 periods)
# corner: self-consistent theory    # -> 4.89e-08 s (245 periods; MC/theory = 0.88)
# identity dt_c·f_{1/f^3}           # -> 0.0489 (= 1/(2×bracket), bracket = 10.22)
# bin sum vs log form (N=10⁴)       # -> 1.089 (f_l=1/T_rec); 0.984 (half-bin correction f_l/2)
# hardware f_l=1 Hz local slope     # -> 0.967 (Δt=1e-7 s; the paper's clean slope-1 fit is justified)
# [P2] osc-12 corner                # -> 6.11e-08 s (171 periods @2.8 GHz)
# implied f_{1/f^3}                 # -> 5.21e+05 Hz (f_l=1 Hz, bracket=15.7)

(Where the 9% bin-sum vs log-form difference comes from: the log closed form takes fl=1/Trecf_l=1/T_{rec}fl​=1/Trec​ as the lower limit of a continuous integral, while the first bin of the discrete FFT spectrum actually collects the power of [fl/2, 3fl/2][f_l/2,\,3f_l/2][fl​/2,3fl​/2] — replacing flf_lfl​ by the half-bin-corrected fl/2f_l/2fl​/2 moves the ratio to 0.984. The log's sluggishness once more: half a bin moves only 9%.)

How to read the figure: the left column shows the three kernels (log-log); you can directly see the low-frequency behavior — TIE flat, period ∝f2\propto f^2∝f2, c2c ∝f4\propto f^4∝f4 — and the peak values 4/16. The middle column shows the MC σΔϕ(N)\sigma_{\Delta\phi}(N)σΔϕ​(N) landing on the κNT\kappa\sqrt{NT}κNT​ theory line (slope 1/2, spanning 4 decades). The right column shows the period and c2c histograms: Gaussian, and σc2c=2 σP\sigma_{c2c}=\sqrt2\,\sigma_Pσc2c​=2​σP​. This is a pedagogical simulation (single white noise source, linear phase accumulation), not transistor-level.

Reconciliation with Example C3 / Example D: the 27.6 fs of worked_examples Example C3 = the closed-form 28.28 fs with the tail above 101010^{10}1010 Hz cut off (there the kernel averages 2 and the 1/f21/f^21/f2 spectrum still contributes ~5% of the variance); the 5.6 fs of psd_phase_noise_jitter Example D is the same kernel integrated only over the 1–100 MHz band. Same set of formulas, same prefactor 1/ω021/\omega_0^21/ω02​ — all three numbers check out.

Key takeaways​

  • One convention all the way: one-sided SϕS_\phiSϕ​ (rad²/Hz), ∫0∞\int_0^\infty∫0∞​, prefactor 1/ω021/\omega_0^21/ω02​. The "2/ω022/\omega_0^22/ω02​" version belongs to the two-sided-spectrum or L\mathcal{L}L bookkeeping — switching bookkeeping means switching the entire formula.
  • Three jitters = 0th/1st/2nd-order differences of ϕ\phiϕ; kernels =1=1=1, 4sin⁡2(πfNT)4\sin^2(\pi fNT)4sin2(πfNT), 16sin⁡4(πfT)16\sin^4(\pi fT)16sin4(πfT). Every 2 has a pedigree: the 2 from the variance of a difference × the 2 from the half-angle identity (squared again to give 16).
  • Rigorous validity of the kernel formulas only requires stationary frequency noise (boxcar derivation); random-walk phase is covered.
  • Punchline: inserting white FM into kernel (b) gives exactly σΔϕ2(N)=κ2NT\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2(N)=\kappa^2NTσΔϕ2​(N)=κ2NT — the frequency-domain kernel picture and the time-domain random walk of [P2] Eq.(8)/(11)/(12) are one and the same thing; MC ratios 0.999–1.001.
  • σc2c=2 σP\sigma_{c2c}=\sqrt2\,\sigma_Pσc2c​=2​σP​ (white noise only); κ=2πΔfLlin\kappa=2\pi\Delta f\sqrt{\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}}κ=2πΔfLlin​​ (remember to use the /2/2/2-convention L\mathcal{L}L: −145-145−145, not −148-148−148).
  • Flicker: σΔϕ2(N)=4π2b3(NT)2[32−γ−ln⁡(2πNTfl)]\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2(N)=4\pi^2b_3(NT)^2[\tfrac32-\gamma-\ln(2\pi NTf_l)]σΔϕ2​(N)=4π2b3​(NT)2[23​−γ−ln(2πNTfl​)], logarithmically dependent on the low-frequency cutoff; a report must include flf_lfl​; the growth law is approximately ∝N\propto N∝N (the slope-1 segment of [P2] Eq.(9)).
  • The two-regime whole picture ([P2] Fig.16): σ(Δt)=κ2Δt+ζ2Δt2\sigma(\Delta t)=\sqrt{\kappa^2\Delta t+\zeta^2\Delta t^2}σ(Δt)=κ2Δt+ζ2Δt2​ (independent ⇒ variances add), corner Δtc=κ2/ζ2\Delta t_c=\kappa^2/\zeta^2Δtc​=κ2/ζ2; time↔frequency mapping Δtc=1/(2[⋅]f1/f3)\Delta t_c=1/(2[\cdot]f_{1/f^3})Δtc​=1/(2[⋅]f1/f3​) with [⋅]≈10[\cdot]\approx10[⋅]≈10–161616 ⇒ 20–30× shorter than 1/f1/f31/f_{1/f^3}1/f1/f3​; osc-12: 61 ns (171 periods), canonical: 49 ns (245 periods); MC slopes 0.519/0.909 = the exact curve's 0.520/0.911 (the deviations from 0.5/1.0 are log physics).
  • Canonical numbers: representative oscillator κ2=0.125\kappa^2=0.125κ2=0.125 rad²/s, σP=0.159\sigma_P=0.159σP​=0.159 fs, σc2c=0.225\sigma_{c2c}=0.225σc2c​=0.225 fs, L(1MHz)=−145/−148\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-145/-148L(1MHz)=−145/−148 dBc/Hz (/2/2/2, /4/4/4 conventions); Example C spectrum: TIE(1–100 MHz)=447.9=447.9=447.9 fs, period-jitter closed form 28.2828.2828.28 fs (Example C3's 27.6 fs is the band-truncated value).
